title: Bridging functional and network robustness
text:
The role of a species in a community can be defined in three ways: where the species is in the functional space, where the species is in the ecological network, and what is the impact of the species loss. These are three lenses with which we can look at a species. They are usually used separately. Yet, they all are an attempt to capture the very same reality. So we argue that to improve our view on a species role in a community it is best to pile up these lenses than using them separately. They are complementary facets and understanding the relationships between these different view enable a more complete view of a role played by a species within a community.



To what degree do a species position in functional trait space, its structural position in the interaction network, and its contribution to community robustness converge or diverge? What does that tell us about community robustness?





Coux et al. (2016) established that functional originality correlates with network specialisation in pollinators. But the why remains underexplored. Traits govern which interactions are possible, such as morphological matching between flower and pollinators. So the trait–network relationship is not merely correlative but mechanistic. A promising direction is to move beyond summary axes (PCoA) and ask which specific traits drive which network metrics. Disentangling these trait-by-metric relationships would give the correlation a mechanistic foundation.



A key question whether functional originality of the lost species determines the magnitude of that loss. If a species is functionally original and topologically central, does its removal trigger a disproportionate cascade? Or do these two dimensions predict different things?



Coux et al. (2016) worked exclusively with plant-pollinator networks, an extension is to test whether the same framework holds in other interaction types — food webs, seed dispersal networks — where the trait–interaction link operates differently. If the relationship between functional position and network role is general, it points to a universal principle of community organisation. If it is system-specific, that contrast itself becomes informative about how different ecological architectures buffer or amplify the consequences of species loss.

title: Bridging functional and network robustness
text:
Framework

Conceptual overview
We decompose the question of species robustness into three interconnected facets: functional trait space position, structural network role, and extinction dynamics. Our analysis links these facets at the species level across empirical plant–pollinator networks (Coux et al. 2016).

Figure 1: Literature landscape showing three research fields and their partial connections. Network ecology and functional diversity have been partially bridged through studies linking trait space position to network structure. Functional diversity and robustness connect through functional redundancy concepts. Network ecology and robustness link via structural importance measures. These three perspectives remain to be integrated all at the same time.







Data and species descriptors
From each network we extract three types of species-level descriptors.
Trait-space descriptors (following Coux et al. (2016); Violle et al. (2017)) summarise a species’ position in its own functional trait space

functional originality, that is, the distance of species \(i\) to the community centroid in PCoA trait space
functional uniqueness, that is, distance to the nearest neighbour in trait space

Network metrics characterise structural embeddedness in the interaction network

degree \(k_i\)
Blüthgen’s \(d'_i\) (Blüthgen et al. 2006), that is, the deviation of interaction distribution from random given partner abundances

Interaction niche metrics (following Dehling and Stouffer (2018); Dehling et al. (2022)) characterise a species through the traits of its interaction partners

interaction niche position, that is, the centroid of species \(i\) in partner trait space
interaction niche size, that is, the hypervolume spanned by interaction partners in trait space
interaction niche originality, that is, distance of species \(i\)’s interaction centroid from the community mean interaction centroid



Extinction simulation
We simulate pollinator extinctions using both a topological coextinction model (Memmott et al. 2004) and a stochastic coextinction model (Vieira and Almeida-Neto 2015), implemented via the bipartite package (Dormann et al. 2008) in R.
For each species \(i\) and each network, we compute three per-species extinction impact metrics
\[\Delta R_i = R_{\text{full}} - R_{-i}\]
where \(R_{-i}\) is network robustness when species \(i\) is removed first,
\[\text{cascade}_i = \mathbb{E}[\text{secondary extinctions triggered by
removal of } i]\]
averaged over 1000 stochastic realisations, and
\[\Delta \text{FD}_i = \text{FD}_{\text{full}} - \text{FD}_{-i}\]
the loss of plant functional diversity following removal of \(i\) and its downstream secondary extinctions.
Simulations are run under three extinction sequences – random, least-to-most-abundant, specialist-to-generalist – to assess robustness of conclusions to sequence choice.


Causal structure and statistical model
The predictors above are not causally independent. A species’ own traits constrain which plants it can interact with (trait matching), which determines its network degree and specialisation, which in turn shapes its interaction niche size and modularity role. We therefore adopt a structural equation modelling which accounts for the causal structure.





flowchart TD
  O[Position in the trait space] --> D[Embedding in the network]
  D --> N[Interacting niche size]
  N --> R[Contribution to robustness]
  O --> R






The hypothesised causal graph contains four paths

originality → degree [trait matching]
degree → interaction niche size [bridging Eltonian niche and functional diversity]
interaction niche size → \(\Delta R\)
originality → \(\Delta R\) [functional redundancy]

title: Bridging functional and network robustness
text:
Other ideas

Invasive species
Link with invasive species. Invasive species may have a high trait uniqueness which make them able of taking a place that is not fulfilled in the pristine community. That is, can we link the position of the invasive species in the trait space to its probability to invade? In the same vein, can we also relate the position in the trait space of the invasive species to its impact on the community?

title: Network and Traits Project
text:
A species’ role in a community can be read through three lenses: its position in functional trait space, its structural position in the interaction network, and its contribution to community robustness. These lenses are usually studied separately, yet they capture the same underlying reality.
This project asks: to what degree do a species’ trait position, network position, and contribution to robustness converge or diverge — and what does that tell us about community robustness? We build on the correlation between functional originality and network specialisation established by (Coux et al. 2016), and aim to give it a mechanistic and predictive foundation using extinction simulations and structural equation modelling.

Interactions
Here is what the raw data looks like.
The columns correspond to

site: the community (21 sites)
pollinator: the pollinator species (16 species across all sites)
plant: the plant species (14 species across all sites)
links: the number of interaction events (visits) observed between that plant and that pollinator at that site (61% show zero observed visits).







Note



data_coux is already cleaned by clean_coux_data(): species names are lowercased everywhere (pollinator names are capitalised and plant names inconsistently so in the raw data), and alnus_glutinosa/alnus_serrulate are merged into a single alnus_sp. The raw interaction table has alnus_glutinosa at site blahamlak with no matching trait/abundance row, and alnus_serrulate at crobirlee/crostelee joining fine. Since no site uses both names, we treat all three as the same plant recorded under two names. See clean_coux_data() in R/analyse-coux.R for details; use tar_read(data_coux_raw) to see the uncleaned version.

Site richness


Code
site_richness <- data$interaction |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(
    pollinator = n_distinct(pollinator),
    plant = n_distinct(plant),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(pollinator, plant),
    names_to = "guild",
    values_to = "n_species"
  ) |>
  mutate(site = fct_reorder(site, n_species, .fun = sum))

ggplot(site_richness, aes(x = site, y = n_species, fill = guild)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of species", fill = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")









Sites range from a few species to much richer communities. Network size itself is a potential confound to keep in mind in later analyses. We also note that plant and pollinator richness are strongly positively correlated.

Degree distribution by guild


Code

  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = "Degree (number of partners)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Degree per species
As for uniqueness and originality above, each species has one degree value per site it occurs at, so we look at the per-species distribution across sites, ordered by median within each guild.


Code
degree_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, degree, .fun = median))

ggplot(degree_by_species, aes(x = species, y = degree, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Degree (number of partners)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Normalised degree per species
Raw degree is mechanically capped by how many species a site has at all, so we also look at normalised degree — degree scaled by the number of possible partners at that site — which partially controls for that site-richness confound.


Code
ndegree_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, normalised_degree, .fun = median))

ggplot(ndegree_by_species, aes(x = species, y = normalised_degree, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Normalised degree") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Specialisation (d′) per species
Same, for Blüthgen’s d′. d′ is NA for species in the three smallest networks (all of a species’ partners are only ever visited by it, leaving the normalisation undefined), which median()/the boxplot silently drop.


Code
dprime_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, d_prime, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(dprime_by_species, aes(x = species, y = d_prime, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Specialisation (Blüthgen's d′)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Specificity (HS) per species
HS is the Shannon-based specificity used by Coux et al. (2016), from Poisot’s ESM package:
\[ \text{HS}_i = 1 - \frac{H_i}{\log R} \]
where \(H_i\) is the Shannon entropy of species \(i\)’s visits across plants and \(R\) is the number of plants visited by anyone at the site. A species with a single partner has HS = 1 (a perfect specialist); one spreading its visits evenly over every available plant has HS = 0. Unlike d′, it does not correct for how often each partner is visited overall. See compute_hs().


Code
hs_by_species <- net_metrics |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, hs, .fun = median))

ggplot(hs_by_species, aes(x = species, y = hs, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Specificity (HS)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

The richest site, for a sense of what an actual interaction web looks like.

richest_site <- names(web_list)[which.max(vapply(web_list, sum, numeric(1)))]

plotweb(
  web_list[[richest_site]],
  higher_color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]],
  lower_color = guild_colors[["plant"]],
  link_color = "grey80",
  srt = 0,
  text_size = 1
)

title: Explore data of Coux et al. 2016
text:
Uniqueness and originality

Uniqueness
We compute species uniqueness per species per site. Uniqueness is defined as
\[ \text{uniqueness}_i = \min_j d_{ij} \]
that is the minimal functional distance to another species present in the community. Following Coux et al. (2016), \(d_{ij}\) is the Euclidean distance in the Cailliez-corrected PCoA space, the same space in which we compute originality below, so that both metrics describe positions in a single trait space. A species alone at its site has no neighbour and is left out.


Code
plant_uniqueness <- tar_read(plant_uniqueness)
pollinator_uniqueness <- tar_read(pollinator_uniqueness)
all_uniqueness <- rbind(
  plant_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pollinator_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
) |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, uniqueness, .fun = median))

ggplot(all_uniqueness, aes(x = species, y = uniqueness, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional uniqueness") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Originality
Functional originality is the distance of a species from the trait centroid of the community it belongs to, i.e. how much its traits differ from the community’s average:
\[ \text{originality}_i = \lVert x_i - \bar{x}_{\text{community}} \rVert \]
We compute it per species per site in the PCoA trait space, with the centroid taken over the species present at each site.


Code
plant_originality <- tar_read(plant_originality)
pollinator_originality <- tar_read(pollinator_originality)
all_originality <- rbind(
  plant_originality |> mutate(guild = "plant"),
  pollinator_originality |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")
) |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, originality, .fun = median))

ggplot(all_originality, aes(x = species, y = originality, fill = guild)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = guild_colors) +
  facet_wrap(~guild, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional originality") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











Weighted originality
Above, the community centroid treats every present species equally. For pollinators we also have abundance data, so we can instead weight the centroid by how common each species is at a site.


Code
pollinator_originality_w <- tar_read(pollinator_originality_w)

originality_comparison <- rbind(
  pollinator_originality |> mutate(weighting = "unweighted"),
  pollinator_originality_w |> mutate(weighting = "weighted by abundance")
) |>
  mutate(
    weighting = factor(
      weighting,
      levels = c("unweighted", "weighted by abundance")
    ),
    species_within = reorder(
      paste(species, weighting, sep = "___"), originality,
      FUN = median
    )
  )

ggplot(
  originality_comparison,
  aes(x = species_within, y = originality, fill = weighting)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "unweighted" = "grey60",
      "weighted by abundance" = guild_colors[["pollinator"]]
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) sub("___.*$", "", x)) +
  facet_wrap(~weighting, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Functional originality") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









We see that ranking shift with weighting. Common generalist, such a_mellifera drop in originality as they pull the community weighted mean, while rarer species such as n_producta increase in originality.
To check, to what extent species abundance drive their originality we plot species weighted originality against their abundance for each site.


Code
pollinator_abundance <- data$pollinator_abundance |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = a_mellifera:t_orthodoxus,
    names_to = "species",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  filter_out(abundance == 0)

originality_abundance <- pollinator_originality_w |>
  left_join(pollinator_abundance, by = join_by(site, species))

ggplot(
  originality_abundance,
  aes(x = log10(abundance), y = originality, color = species),
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Abundance (log10 scale)",
    y = "Weighted originality",
    color = "Species"
  )









We see that there is strong negative correlation between weighted originality and species abundance. This means that we should be careful if we use this metric.

Next, we want to check that species originality and uniqueness are not too strongly correlated, to ensure that the two metrics are complementary description of species position in the functional space.

  pol_originality_uniqueness |> mutate(guild = "pollinator")

ggplot(

text:
Interaction niche
Following Dehling & Stouffer (2018) and Dehling et al. (2022), a species’ interaction niche describes it through the traits of its interaction partners rather than its own traits: its position is the (link-weighted) centroid of its partners’ traits in the partner guild’s trait space, its size is how dispersed those partners are around that centroid, and its originality is how far that centroid sits from the average position of its guild-mates at the same site.
We use dispersion rather than a hull/hypervolume for niche size: partner counts here are low (median degree 1-2.5 per the degree distributions above), too low for a hull-based volume to be defined for most species, whereas a dispersion-based measure degrades gracefully — a species with a single partner simply gets a niche size of 0.

text:
Trait position vs network position
Coux et al. (2016) found that a pollinator’s position in trait space is linked to its position in the network: functionally original pollinators tend to be more specialised. This link is also the first path of our planned SEM (originality → degree). Here we check whether it holds in our data, and whether it holds for the whole pollinator community or comes from A. mellifera alone. The honeybee provides 18 of the 90 pollinator-site rows, and all 18 sit at high originality and high degree.


Code

  mutate(
    focal = if_else(species == "a_mellifera", "A. mellifera", "Other"),
    focal = factor(focal, levels = c("Other", "A. mellifera"))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(originality, uniqueness),
    names_to = "trait_metric", values_to = "trait_value"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(normalised_degree, d_prime),
    names_to = "network_metric", values_to = "network_value"

section: Does originality predict a pollinator’s network role?
text:
Does originality predict a pollinator’s network role?
Coux et al. (2016) report that a pollinator’s functional originality predicts its role in the network: its normalised degree (ND) and its specificity (HS). Their models regress ND and HS on abundance-weighted originality and on abundance, plus a few other terms with small effects that we leave aside here.


Code
pollinator_trait_network <- tar_read(pollinator_trait_network)
trait_network_models <- tar_read(trait_network_models)
trait_network_models_richness <- tar_read(trait_network_models_richness)

# Format a coefficient as "mean [lower, upper]".
coef_text <- function(tbl, response, model, term) {
  row <- tbl[tbl$response == response & tbl$model == model &
    tbl$term == term, ]
  sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", row$mean, row$lower, row$upper)
}
spearman <- function(x, y) {
  sprintf("%.2f", cor(x, y, method = "spearman"))
}



Weighted and unweighted originality
When weighting the community centroid by abundance an abundant species drags the centroid towards itself. The more abundant you are, the closer you sit to the centroid, and the less “original” you look.


Code
originality_vs_abundance <- pollinator_trait_network |>
  select(site, species, abundance, originality, originality_w) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(originality, originality_w),
    names_to = "measure", values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c("originality", "originality_w"),
      labels = c(
        paste0(
          "Unweighted (ρ = ",
          spearman(
            pollinator_trait_network$originality,
            log(pollinator_trait_network$abundance)
          ), ")"
        ),
        paste0(
          "Weighted by abundance (ρ = ",
          spearman(
            pollinator_trait_network$originality_w,
            log(pollinator_trait_network$abundance)
          ), ")"
        )
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(originality_vs_abundance, aes(x = abundance, y = value)) +
  geom_point(color = guild_colors[["pollinator"]], alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Abundance (log scale)", y = "Functional originality")









And so it is. Weighted originality falls with abundance (Spearman ρ = -0.51), while unweighted originality, if anything, rises with it (ρ = 0.38). The two versions of “originality” barely agree on which species are original (ρ = 0.15). They are not two estimates of the same thing. They are two different things with the same name.
Now put weighted originality into a model alongside abundance. Abundance is now on the right-hand side twice: once openly, as a covariate, and once smuggled in through the originality term. The model can’t tell which of the two is doing the work. Whatever abundance does to network role, some of it will be credited to “originality”, and the abundance coefficient will look weaker than it is.


The models
We fit the model of Coux et al. (2016) and the same model with unweighted originality, for both responses:

ND ~ weighted originality + abundance (as in Coux et al.)
ND ~ originality + abundance
and the same two models for HS.

All models are mixed models fitted with INLA, with site and species as random intercepts under PC priors (P(sd > 1) = 0.01).

ND is modelled as a binomial: the number of plants a pollinator visits, out of the plants at its site.
HS is modelled as Gaussian, like the linear mixed models of Coux et al. That’s a crude choice for a measure bounded by 0 and 1, with every single-partner species sitting exactly at 1, but it keeps the comparison with their analysis honest.

Abundance is log-transformed. All predictors are standardised, so coefficients are per standard deviation, on the link scale.

What we learn
Normalised degree. Both versions of originality point the same way: original pollinators visit a smaller share of the plants around them. The estimate is -0.31 [-0.57, -0.06] with weighted originality and -0.25 [-0.54, 0.05] with unweighted originality. So the result of Coux et al. replicates with their measure. With the trait-only measure, the effect is smaller and its interval just includes zero.
Now look at abundance. Its coefficient is 0.50 [0.20, 0.81] in the unweighted model, but only 0.31 [0.01, 0.62] in the weighted one. That’s what you’d predict if weighted originality is partly a stand-in for abundance: it takes some of the credit for what abundance does. Abundance matters for ND for a boring but important reason: the more individuals you watch, the more of their partners you record.
Can model fit settle which version is right? No. WAIC barely separates the two models (differences of a unit or two). We shouldn’t expect it to: both models contain roughly the same information, just split differently between the two predictors. The case for unweighted originality is conceptual, not statistical: we want “originality” to describe a species’ position in trait space, and not how common it is.
Specificity (HS). Neither version of originality predicts HS (weighted: 0.03 [-0.05, 0.10]; unweighted: -0.03 [-0.11, 0.06]). Only abundance does: abundant pollinators are a little less specialised (-0.11 [-0.19, -0.03]).
That’s odd at first sight, because ND and HS are closely related (Spearman ρ = -0.89). How can originality predict one but not the other? The clue is in the denominators. ND divides by the number of plants at the site, so it falls as sites get richer (ρ = -0.31). HS is scaled by the log of the number of plants at the site, and barely varies with plant richness (ρ = -0.04). Which suggests that site size is doing some of the work in the ND models.


What about site size?
Both models have a site random intercept, so you might think site size is already taken care of. It isn’t, for two reasons. First, many sites have only two or three pollinators, so each site’s effect is estimated from very few records and is pulled towards zero. Second, and more important, originality itself varies between sites: it is higher at plant-rich sites (ρ = 0.29), where ND is mechanically lower because it is divided by more plants. So some of the between-site difference in ND flows into the originality coefficient. A site random intercept can’t stop that. A fixed effect of plant richness can, so we add log plant richness to both models.

The weighted originality used by Coux et al. (2016) is partly a measure of abundance. In a model that also includes abundance, it takes some of the credit for abundance’s effect. That doesn’t make the result of Coux et al. wrong, but it makes it hard to read as a statement about traits.
With unweighted originality, a trait-only measure, the effect on ND is weaker, and about half of it goes away once plant richness is accounted for.

title: Species contributions to robustness and functional diversity
text: We measure what each pollinator contributes to its community, to later ask with a structural equation model how much of that contribution depends on its network role (normalised degree) and its position in trait space (originality). We measure each pollinator’s contribution to:

title: Species contributions to robustness and functional diversity
text:
Contribution to robustness
We remove a pollinator and see what happens to the plants. Two candidate metrics.

Candidate 1: cascading extinctions
Remove pollinator \(i\); any plant left without a pollinator goes extinct (topological coextinction, Memmott et al. 2004). The cascade can’t go further: a pollinator dies only once all its plants are dead, but a plant dies only once all its pollinators are gone, including that one. So
\[\text{cascade}_i = \text{number of plants whose only pollinator is } i\]
Easy to read, but coarse: in most networks, losing one pollinator kills no plant.


Candidate 2: shift in robustness
Robustness \(R\) is the area under the curve of the fraction of plants surviving as pollinators are removed one by one (Burgos et al. 2007). It ranges from near 0 (plants collapse early) to 1 (plants survive until the last pollinator goes). The contribution of \(i\) is
\[\Delta R_i = R_{\text{full}} - R^{\text{first}}_i\]
where \(R_{\text{full}}\) is averaged over random removal orders and \(R^{\text{first}}_i\) over the same orders with \(i\) moved to the front. It asks: how much worse is it to lose \(i\) first than an average pollinator? Unlike the cascade, it also captures plants left with a single pollinator, which die earlier later on.
Still open: the stochastic coextinction model of Vieira and Almeida-Neto (2015), where a plant dies with a probability that grows with the share of interactions it has lost, would give smoother contributions, at the cost of one parameter.

title: Species contributions to robustness and functional diversity
text:
Contribution to functional diversity
We measure plant functional diversity (FD) with a dendrogram (Petchey and Gaston 2002): an average-linkage (UPGMA) tree of the 14 plant species in trait space, the same space as for originality. The FD of a set of plants is the total length of the branches connecting them, so a single plant has FD = 0. We build one tree for all sites, so branch lengths are comparable between sites.
Below, P. marginata is the only pollinator of Lolium at daiburnam. Losing it costs a third of the plants but half of the FD, because Lolium sits alone on a long branch.

We then repeat the robustness calculation with the fraction of the site’s plant FD retained instead of the fraction of plants alive. \(\Delta FD_i\) is defined like \(\Delta R_i\), with the same removal orders (compute_fd_contributions() in R/contributions.R). It also sums to zero within a site.

  mutate(fd_residual = resid(fd_fit))


A pollinator removes FD only through the plants it alone visits, so \(\Delta FD_i\) closely follows \(\Delta R_i\) (R² = 0.97, slope = 1.10; dashed line 1:1 below). The slope is above 1 because the last plant has FD = 0, so FD falls faster than the number of plants. We use the residual of the regression, rather than the raw difference \(\Delta FD_i - \Delta R_i\), so that it does not depend on \(\Delta R_i\). It is positive when the plants \(i\) supports are functionally distinct, and negative when they have functional equivalents at the site.

title: Species contributions to robustness and functional diversity
text:
Structural equation model
We ask how a pollinator’s traits shape its contribution to plant FD by going through the network. The variables sit on two axes, trait space vs network and pollinator vs plant:









Pollinator
Plant




Trait space
breadth, position
breadth and position of the plants visited


Network
normalised degree
\(\Delta R_i\): the plants that depend on \(i\)



with \(\Delta FD_i\) as the outcome: how many plants depend on \(i\) (\(\Delta R_i\)), and which ones (their position). Paths only run along an axis:

down (traits set network roles): a broad pollinator meets more plants, a peripheral one fewer; a narrow or peripheral plant has fewer pollinators, so it depends more on each;
across (pollinators shape plants): a peripheral pollinator visits peripheral plants (trait matching); a narrow pollinator can only reach broad plants; the degree of a pollinator sets how many plants depend on it.

This structure follows from a trait-matching model in which plants and pollinators interact when their niches overlap (Trait-matching model).
We take every trait from the Coux trait tables. Breadth is a single trait per guild, chosen a priori as the classic marker of generalism:

pollinators: sociality. Social bees maintain colonies over a long season, so they forage across many flowering periods and collect from whatever flowers are open. Only A. mellifera and B. terrestris are social, so pollinator breadth here cannot be separated from these two species. Sociality also predicts normalised degree in these data, while body size, the other candidate (larger pollinators forage further), does not;
plants: inflorescence symmetry. Radially symmetric (actinomorphic) inflorescences are open to many pollinators, whereas bilaterally symmetric (zygomorphic) ones restrict access to pollinators of matching shape and behaviour, the textbook marker of specialised pollination. We use the inflorescence, the unit pollinators land on, rather than the single flower: the heads of Taraxacum, Cirsium or Trifolium are made of zygomorphic florets but are open, radially symmetric resources.

Breadth could instead be measured from the interactions, as the trait diversity of a species’ partners. In these sparse networks this mostly measures degree: a species with a single partner has zero breadth, which is the case for a third of the pollinator records and half of the plants. Measured at the other sites, to break this circularity, it does not predict degree. Position is originality, for both guilds: the pollinator’s, and the mean of the plants it visits. Plant uniqueness explains \(\Delta FD_i\) slightly better (see above), but in the model originality carries the link between pollinator and plant positions far better.
We fit a piecewise SEM (Lefcheck 2016), with one glmmTMB mixed model per response: binomial for normalised degree, Gaussian otherwise, with random effects of site and species, and correlated errors between the breadth and position of the plants visited (fit_grid_sem() in R/sem.R).

sem_summary <- tar_read(contribution_sem_summary)
sem_coefs <- sem_summary$coefficients
sem_est <- function(response, predictor) {
  row <- sem_coefs$Response == response & sem_coefs$Predictor == predictor
  p <- sem_coefs$P.Value[row]
  sprintf(
    "%+.2f, %s", sem_coefs$Std.Estimate[row],
    if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", p)
  )
}

missing <- sem_summary$dTable
missing_p <- function(claim) {
  sprintf("%.2f", missing$P.Value[startsWith(missing$Independ.Claim, claim)])
}




Code

  tar_read(contribution_sem), sem_data,
  breadth_label = "Sociality", plant_breadth_label = "Open inflorescences\nvisited"
)









Arrows show standardised coefficients (plot_sem_paths() in R/sem.R; 89 records, 16 species). The model fits (Fisher’s C = 24.9, df = 20, p = 0.21).

The network row works. Social pollinators have a higher normalised degree (+0.34, p = 0.002), and degree sets how many plants depend on a pollinator (+0.92, p < 0.001), which carries most of \(\Delta FD_i\) (+0.99, p < 0.001). Original pollinators tend to have a lower degree (-0.13, p = 0.064), as in the model.
The trait row fails. Original pollinators do not visit original plants (-0.02, p = 0.875), and social pollinators visit actinomorphic flowers only weakly more (+0.15, p = 0.134).
The plant column is weak. Visiting original plants raises \(\Delta FD_i\) beyond \(\Delta R_i\) (+0.03, p = 0.046), but the breadth of the plants visited does not change \(\Delta R_i\) (+0.10, p = 0.209), whereas in the model narrow plants depend more on their pollinators.

One missing path is flagged, a direct, negative link from pollinator originality to \(\Delta FD_i\) (p = 0.04): original pollinators contribute less to plant FD than their \(\Delta R_i\) and plants predict. A. mellifera and B. terrestris are both the most original and the only social pollinators, and they concentrate on common plant types.
Why the trait row fails. The position argument needs a trait space shared by plants and pollinators, in which distance means “likely to interact”. The Coux traits describe each guild on its own (body size, diet, sociality; growth form, inflorescence, flowering season), and none were collected as matching pairs, such as tongue length and corolla depth. Pairing every pollinator trait with every plant trait, none predicts which pairs interact beyond chance (132 combinations, smallest adjusted p = 0.80). Phenology is the only dimension both guilds share, but each network was sampled within one flowering window, so it cannot show matching. Testing position thus requires matching traits measured on both guilds. With 16 species, two of them introduced social bees at the extreme of most axes, these data also have little power.

title: Trait-matching model
text: We ask how a pollinator’s traits shape its contribution to plant functional diversity, going through the network. The question sits on two axes, trait space vs network and pollinator vs plant, which the SEM of Species contributions makes explicit. In the Coux data, the network row of that SEM works but the trait row does not. Is that what trait matching predicts? We build a minimal trait-matching model, fit the same SEM to simulated networks, and ask how its paths vary with the strength of trait matching, with richness, and with the link between a species’ breadth and its position.

title: Trait-matching model
text:
Model
Plants and pollinators sit in a shared space of two traits, each drawn from a standard normal. Each species also has a niche breadth \(\sigma\), log-normal within its guild. A plant \(i\) and a pollinator \(j\) interact in proportion to the overlap of their Gaussian niches, which decreases with their trait distance \(d_{ij}\):
\[w_{ij} = (1 - \lambda) \frac{e^{-d_{ij}^2 / 2(\sigma_i^2 + \sigma_j^2)}}{\bar w} + \lambda\]
where \(\lambda\) is the share of interactions independent of traits: \(\lambda = 0\) is pure trait matching, \(\lambda = 1\) a random network. This is the trait-matching (“complementarity”) rule of mutualistic network models, with a niche breadth for both guilds. Within each guild, log breadth is correlated with the distance to the guild’s centroid with coefficient \(\rho\): peripheral species are generalists if \(\rho > 0\), specialists if \(\rho < 0\). Links are drawn with probabilities proportional to \(w_{ij}\), scaled so that each plant has 2 pollinators on average. A species left without a partner gets its most likely one. As in Coux, there are about 0.65 pollinators per plant and plants have 2 pollinators on average (simulate_network() in R/simulation.R).
Below, a network under pure trait matching (\(\rho = 0\)): plants (orange squares, sized by breadth) and pollinators (blue dots), with links in grey. Three pollinators are highlighted, with the narrowest, the median and the widest niche (circle of radius \(\sigma_j\)). Broad plants are reached from further away.


Code
plot_simulated_network(tar_read(sim_example))

title: Trait-matching model
text:
Breadth, position and contributions
As in Coux:

breadth is the niche breadth \(\sigma\) (log scale): the pollinator’s, and the mean of the plants it visits;
position is originality, the distance to the centroid of the species’ own guild in trait space: the pollinator’s, and the mean of the plants it visits;
\(\Delta R_i\) and \(\Delta FD_i\) are computed as in Coux, with plant FD from an average-linkage dendrogram of plant traits and 50 random removal orders (simulate_pollinator_data()).

We simulate 30 networks for each combination of \(\lambda \in \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}\), \(\rho \in \{-0.5, 0, 0.5\}\) and 5, 10, 15 or 20 plants (3, 6, 10 and 13 pollinators), the size of the Coux networks.
Why originality for position. Plant uniqueness (distance to the nearest plant) explains \(\Delta FD_i\) beyond \(\Delta R_i\) slightly better than plant originality, but originality carries the matching between pollinator and plant positions far better, because the distance to a centroid is less noisy than the distance to a single neighbour. Under trait matching (\(\lambda = 0\), \(\rho = 0\)), median Spearman correlations across networks:


Code
tar_read(sim_position_metrics) |>
  filter(lambda == 0, rho == 0) |>

title: Trait-matching model
section: The Coux SEM in the model
text:
The Coux SEM in the model
We fit the Coux SEM to batches of 15 simulated networks, like the Coux sites: breadth → normalised degree → \(\Delta R_i\) → \(\Delta FD_i\), and originality → originality of the plants visited → \(\Delta FD_i\), with a site random effect (fit_simulated_sems()). Each setting gives two SEMs. Dashed lines show the Coux estimates.


Code
plot_simulated_sems(
  tar_read(sim_sems), tar_read(contribution_sem_summary)$coefficients
)











Code
sim_sems <- tar_read(sim_sems)
coux <- tar_read(contribution_sem_summary)
mean_std <- function(p, lam) {
  sprintf("%.2f", mean(sim_sems$std[sim_sems$path == p & sim_sems$lambda == lam]))
}
coux_std <- function(p) {
  co <- coux$coefficients
  sprintf("%.2f", co$Std.Estimate[paste(co$Predictor, "->", co$Response) == p])
}
fits <- distinct(sim_sems, n_plants, lambda, batch, fisher_p, missing)



Both trait effects appear under trait matching and fade as it weakens. At \(\lambda = 0\), breadth → degree is 0.40 and originality → plant originality 0.54; both vanish in random networks (0.00 and 0.01 at \(\lambda = 1\)).
Position needs richness, breadth does not. The position link grows with the number of plants (from 0.30 with 5 plants to 0.70 with 80, at \(\lambda = 0\)), as positions are estimated from more species; the breadth link barely changes with richness.
The plant side holds everywhere. Visiting original plants raises \(\Delta FD_i\) beyond \(\Delta R_i\) in every setting, and more so when interactions are less trait-driven.

Coux against the model. In Coux, breadth → degree (0.27) falls where the model has partial trait matching (\(\lambda\) ≈ 0.25–0.5), but originality → plant originality (-0.02) falls where it has none (\(\lambda\) ≈ 1). In the model, breadth and position act in the same trait space, so no single \(\lambda\) gives this combination. The mismatch fits the Coux traits: sociality acts on breadth directly, whereas the trait space in which we measure position does not carry matching. Coux also has stronger degree → \(\Delta R_i\) (0.93) and \(\Delta R_i\) → \(\Delta FD_i\) (0.99) links, and a weaker plant originality → \(\Delta FD_i\) link (0.03), than any simulated setting: its networks are smaller and sparser, which ties the two contributions together.
Missing paths. With hundreds of pollinators per SEM, the d-separation tests reject 43 of 50 simulated SEMs. The paths they flag show that breadth and position are not fully separate in the model:

  count(path, sort = TRUE, name = "SEMs flagging it") |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Missing path", paste("SEMs flagging it, out of", nrow(fits))))

The two most frequent are position effects outside the position branch. Original pollinators have a lower degree: at the edge of trait space, fewer plants are within reach. Pollinators visiting original plants contribute more to robustness: peripheral plants have few visitors, so their pollinators are more often their only one. Coux, with 89 records, has little power to detect these paths.
Below, the SEM for one batch of 15 networks under pure trait matching (\(\lambda = 0\), 20 plants), refitted with these two paths added (highlighted).

Position now acts through both branches: original pollinators have a lower degree, which lowers their contribution to robustness, but they visit original plants, which raises it and raises \(\Delta FD_i\). Even with these paths, this SEM is still rejected (Fisher’s C = 45.6, df = 14, p = <2e-16): with 450 pollinators, the tests also detect smaller direct effects of breadth and originality on \(\Delta R_i\), and of degree on \(\Delta FD_i\).

section: The grid SEM in the model
text:
The grid SEM in the model
We fit the Coux SEM to batches of 15 simulated networks, like the Coux sites, with a site random effect (fit_simulated_sem()). Below, one batch under pure trait matching (\(\lambda = 0\), \(\rho = 0\), 20 plants).


Code
sem_example <- tar_read(sim_sem_example)
example_summary <- summarise_contribution_sem(sem_example$sem, sem_example$data)


Random effect variances not available. Returned R2 does not account for random effects.


Random effect variances not available. Returned R2 does not account for random effects.




Code
plot_sem_paths(sem_example$sem, sem_example$data)









Every path along the two axes is present: breadth and position set degree (down, pollinator), narrow pollinators reach broad plants and peripheral ones peripheral plants (across, trait space), degree sets how many plants depend on the pollinator (across, network), and narrow or peripheral plants depend more on their pollinators (down, plant). With 195 pollinators, the tests still detect smaller paths across the axes (Fisher’s C = 33.7, df = 20, p = 0.028; see below).
How the paths vary with trait matching and richness (\(\rho = 0\); each setting gives two SEMs; dashed lines show the Coux estimates):


Code
sim_sems <- tar_read(sim_sems)
failed <- if ("error" %in% names(sim_sems)) sum(!is.na(sim_sems$error)) else 0
sim_sems <- filter(sim_sems, !is.na(path))
coux <- tar_read(contribution_sem_summary)
sim_mean <- function(p, lam = 0, r = 0, plants = NULL) {
  keep <- sim_sems$path == p & sim_sems$lambda %in% lam & sim_sems$rho %in% r
  if (!is.null(plants)) keep <- keep & sim_sems$n_plants %in% plants
  sprintf("%.2f", mean(sim_sems$std[keep]))
}
coux_std <- function(p) {
  co <- coux$coefficients
  sprintf("%.2f", co$Std.Estimate[paste(co$Predictor, "->", co$Response) == p])
}
fits <- distinct(sim_sems, n_plants, lambda, rho, batch, fisher_p, missing)




Code
plot_simulated_sems(sim_sems, coux$coefficients, colour_by = "n_plants")










Every trait path needs trait matching. All paths from traits fade to zero as interactions become random (e.g. breadth → degree, from 0.34 at \(\lambda = 0\) to -0.01 at \(\lambda = 1\)). The network row (degree → \(\Delta R_i\) → \(\Delta FD_i\)) and plant position → \(\Delta FD_i\) hold at any \(\lambda\): they follow from how the contributions are built.
Breadth paths have the signs of niche overlap. Narrow pollinators reach broad plants (breadth → plant breadth, -0.38), and pollinators visiting narrow plants contribute more to robustness (plant breadth → \(\Delta R_i\), -0.17): narrow plants depend more on each pollinator.
Position needs richness, breadth does not. Position → plant position rises from 0.15 with 5 plants to 0.38 with 20, as positions are estimated from more species; breadth paths barely change.

How the paths vary with the breadth-position correlation (averaged over richness):


Code
plot_simulated_sems(sim_sems, coux$coefficients, colour_by = "rho")










When peripheral species are specialists (\(\rho < 0\)), position matching vanishes (position → plant position, 0.02 at \(\lambda = 0\), against 0.29 at \(\rho = 0\)): a peripheral specialist only reaches the few plants next to it, which need not be peripheral themselves.
\(\rho\) sets the breadth-position correlation of the plants visited, which the SEM absorbs as correlated errors; the other paths change little.

Coux against the model. Coux matches the model under trait matching on the pollinator column and the network row: breadth → degree (0.34; model at \(\lambda = 0\): 0.34), position → degree (-0.13; -0.13), and a stronger network row. It departs on the trait row and the plant column. Position → plant position (-0.02) is what the model gives without trait matching (\(\lambda = 1\): -0.03). The two plant-breadth paths are weak and positive where the model has them negative: breadth → plant breadth 0.15 (model -0.38) and plant breadth → \(\Delta R_i\) 0.10 (model -0.17). The Coux pollinator traits behave as trait matching predicts; the plant traits we used (inflorescence symmetry for breadth, the full trait table for position) do not.
Missing paths. With hundreds of pollinators per SEM, the d-separation tests reject 62 of 120 simulated SEMs, more often in richer networks. The paths they flag cross the two axes:
